title: Comparison of Warm and Cold Forging with Friction Welding for Inner Constant Velocity Joints (CVJs)
abstract: Abstract Driveshafts are used in all vehicles, and their service life is expected to be at least three years or 100.000 km. Many driveshaft manufacturers prefer friction welding due to its relatively cheaper cost and ease of the process. However, they should meet some property-related criteria to achieve the expected lifetime. The forging technique becomes essential to succeed in these mechanical requirements. A comparative study evaluates the performance of constant velocity joints (CVJs) produced by multi-step warm–cold forging and friction welding processes. Medium carbon steels were used in both of the techniques. The microstructures, mechanical properties (i.e. hardness, strength, impact energy and shear strength), low-cycle fatigue (LCF) properties, wear resistance and cost-efficiency (number of operations, material saving, number of produced components and cost) are compared in detail for an industrial production point of view. The experimental results reveal that warm–cold forged specimens exhibit superior mechanical properties such as increased strength, hardness, relatively higher impact energy, improved shear strength, relatively longer LCF life and enhanced wear resistance (lower wear volume loss). In addition, it is also assessed that warm–cold forging is a more cost-effective manufacturing process (reduced weight, decreased number of operations and increased yield) in the production of CVJs compared to the friction welding process.
journal: Transactions of the Indian Institute of Metals

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: A driveshaft is a power transmission component that transfers the power from the engine to the wheels. Driveshafts are composed of many subcomponents and can mainly be divided into three main parts: (i) inner constant velocity joint (CVJ), (ii) outer constant velocity joint and (iii) shafts between inner and outer CVJ. Inner CVJs are mostly assembled directly to the transmission, whereas outer CVJs are assembled to the wheel hub. The inner CVJs, which are located on the right-hand side, contain a stem part connected to them due to the wheel distance [ 1 ]. The inner CVJs can be manufactured with two techniques: (i) friction welding and (ii) direct forging. In friction welding, the body side (CVJ side) is independently forged and then joined to the stem with friction welding [ 2 ,  3 ,  4 ,  5 – 6 ]. In the second technique, the inner CVJs are manufactured by subsequent warm and cold forging processes without any welding [ 7 ,  8 ,  9 ,  10 – 11 ]. Both methods use hot-rolled medium carbon steel ingots as raw material. The manufacturing process finishes with machining and proper heat-treatment operations.

The rising universal demand in the fabrication of near-net-shape parts such as CVJs improves enhanced warm and cold forging [ 6 ,  12 ]. Cold forging is a famous manufacturing process with a high production rate used to produce parts with complex geometries having excellent tolerances and mechanical properties as the parts are forged under the materials’ recrystallization temperature [ 12 ,  13 ]. The main mechanism of the improved properties is driven by the generated dislocations due to the high flow stresses of the cold forging. The cold forging process's other advantages are the lack of surface degradation, scale/oxide formation and thermal expansion. The main drawback of warm–cold forging from an industrial application of view is the requirement of the high initial investment cost due to the high tonnage presses and skilled engineers to design the necessary forging tools. Compared to cold forging, warm forging offers reduced press loads and flow stress of the material [ 12 ,  14 ,  15 ,  16 ,  17 – 18 ]. The high investment cost disadvantage of the production technique can be overcome by mass production so as to produce economic parts [ 6 ,  7 ,  10 ].

The warm and cold forging of inner CVJs having long stem portions requires multiple tooling, design and finite element analysis (FEA) periods to achieve excellent dimensional tolerances. However, from an industrial point of view, producing inner CVJs with friction welding, which can be applied to dissimilar carbon steel joints [ 19 ], is a more straightforward method and contains extensive machining operations before and after the welding. Prior to welding, the surfaces should be perpendicular to the rotation axis and must be cleaned of any contamination, such as grease and protective films of rust or oxides. Compared to conventional fusion welding methods, friction welding has important advantages: (i) less heat input, (ii) better mechanical properties, (iii) non-formation of adverse phase transformations and (iv) more environmentally friendly (no fume or spatter) [ 20 ,  21 ,  22 – 23 ]. Although the friction welding process is much easier, the components' resultant mechanical and structural properties are worse. Moreover, geometrical restrictions of components, wider dimensional tolerances and massive material deposition seem to be the main drawbacks of the friction welding process [ 6 ,  24 ]. The only merit of the friction welding of such components from an industrial application point of view is the relatively low investment.

On the other hand, the correct choice of cost-effective manufacturing process is also a critical factor in today’s competitive industry. Production of high-quality components exhibiting excellent tolerances, dimensional stability and superior surface conditions at low cost requires fewer and more effective processes, eliminating some secondary or intermediate operations and reducing weight [ 25 ]. In the context of inner CVJs manufacturing, warm and cold forging seems more efficient in terms of cost-efficiency, physical and mechanical properties, and minimal material waste when compared with friction welding.

In this study, the mechanical properties, microstructure, fatigue and torsion properties, wear behaviour and cost-efficiency (number of operations, material saving, number of produced components and cost) of warm–cold forged inner CVJs with long stems are compared with the friction-welded counterparts.

sections.heading: Friction Welding on Inner CVJ
paragraphs: In the friction welding process, DIN Ck45 steel is used for the stem, and DIN Cf53 steel is used for the CVJ. The chemical compositions of these steels, analysed with OBLF RS1000-162 model optical emission spectrometer (OES), are shown in Table  1 . Table 1 Chemical compositions of the steels used Material Chemical composition (wt. %) C Si Mn P S DIN Cf53 0.57 0.22 0.62 0.007 0.005 DIN Ck45 0.46 0.20 0.63 0.011 0.024

Both parts are machined to Ø 37.5 mm for friction welding. The stem is clamped with a hydraulic vise, and the CVJ is fixed with a rotating chuck. As shown in Fig.  1 a, axial movement and pressure are applied from the stem side to the CVJ side while the CVJ side rotates and remains stationary during the process. Figure  1 b shows the machine used in the friction welding process. The friction welding machine applies a maximum force of 10 tons and works with a hydraulic system. Peripheral speed adjustment is manual and provided by gear shifts. PLC system is available, and the process is under control with pressure control. Fig. 1 a  Schematic representation of friction welding, and  b  friction welding machine

The process parameters used in the friction welding process are shown in Table  2 . Fixed support is used for the overall length limitation of 10 mm. 1065 rpm is adjusted by shifting the gear system to provide 2.1 m/s circumferential speed. To adjust the friction pressure and forging pressure, the hydraulic pressures of the machine are adjusted to 45 bars for friction and 90 bars for forging. Table 2 Friction welding parameters Friction welding parameters Value Velocity 2.1 m/s Friction pressure 4 kgf/mm 2 Forging pressure 8 kgf/mm 2 Friction length 8.5 mm Forging length 1.5 mm Total length shortening 10 mm

sections.heading: Warm and Cold Forging of Inner CVJ
paragraphs: DIN Cf53 material, widely applied in automotive axle systems [ 26 ], is used in this study. The process steps of warm and cold forging are shown in Fig.  2 . Op1–2 are the warm forging operations, and Op3–4–5 are the cold forging operations. The billet diameter is Ø 45 mm, and its length is 356 mm. The warm forging process takes place at 760 °C. After locally heating the billet, upsetting and back extrusion processes are employed. 250 tons and 630 tons of hydraulic presses are used for Op1 and Op2, respectively. Fig. 2 Production steps of warm and cold forged CVJs

Annealing, sandblasting and coating processes are carried out after the warm forging to prepare the material for cold forging. Annealing is carried out for 2 h in a continuous furnace at 680 °C. After annealing, sandblasting and Zn-Stearate coating are carried out. There are six baths in the coating process. These are acid, rinse, activation, phosphate, passivation and stearate baths. In the first step of the cold forging part, which is Op3, all the details of the CVJ part are finalised. Then, this process is followed by cold extrusion of the stem with Op4 and Op5. In Op5, a double cold extrusion process is performed. The process parameters of the forging operations are given in Table  3 . Table 3 Forging process parameters Press type Velocity Stroke Operations 250 tons hydraulic press 200 mm/s 500 mm Op1-Op3 630 tons hydraulic press 130 mm/s 500 mm Op2-Op4-Op5

sections.heading: Mechanical Tests
paragraphs: The mechanical properties of the forged and welded samples are investigated by tensile, impact, torsion and microhardness tests. Tensile tests are conducted using a 600-kN Dartec universal testing equipment at a strain rate of 10 –4  s −1  according to ISO 6892–1: 2016 standard (Metallic materials Tensile testing Part 1: Method of test at room temperature) [ 27 ]. The 0.2% proof stress in uniaxial tension is considered the yield stress. Two specimens are tested for each condition. The tensile test samples are machined from the forged and welded samples, as shown in Fig.  3 a, b. Figure  3 c shows the dimensions of the tensile test specimen. For forged ones (Fig.  3 a), the specimen called F1 is obtained from the single forged part, and the specimen F2 is obtained from the double-forged part. The tensile test specimen for the welded one is obtained from the friction-welded region. The rectangular notched Charpy specimens of 10 × 10 × 55 mm dimensions are tested using an ALSA ZBC 300 model impact test machine according to the ASTM E23 standard (Standard Test Methods for Notched Bar Impact Testing of Metallic Materials) [ 28 ]. Fig. 3 Locations of the tension test samples in the  a  warm–cold forged, and  b  friction- welded CVJ;  c  dimensions and geometry of the tension test sample (mm)

Vickers microhardness measurements are performed utilising a Buehler Wilson VH1202 model microhardness tester on the forged and welded samples (polished with 1 µm alumina solution) with an applied load of 10 g for 5 s. The indentation points for the Vickers microhardness measurements are shown in Fig.  4 . For the forged and welded samples, microhardness measurements (Fig.  4 a) are performed on 25 independent points placed at a distance of 3 mm in length and 3 mm in width. For the welded sample (Fig.  4 b), 100 independent indentations are performed. Moreover, the hardness map for the welded sample is generated using MATLAB software. Fig. 4 Indentation points for the Vickers microhardness test,  a  forged sample and  b  welded sample

Torsion tests are performed to determine the shear strength of forged and welded samples. Torsion test specimens are obtained from forged and welded samples according to ISO 18338:2021 standard (Metallic materials—Torsion test at room temperature) [ 29 ], as shown in Fig.  5 a, b. The dimensions of the test specimens are shown in Fig.  5 c. Torsion tests are performed using a 200-Nm capacity TecQuipment SM21 model apparatus (Fig.  5 d). The tests are carried out at room temperature with 60% humidity. Fig. 5 Locations of the torsion test samples in the  a  warm–cold forged, and  b  friction- welded CVJ;  c  dimensions and geometry of the torsion test sample (mm), and  d  torsion test equipment

sections.heading: Fatigue Tests
paragraphs: Strain-controlled low-cycle fatigue (LCF) tests are performed to estimate and compare the fatigue life of forged and welded samples. The fatigue life of the specimens is determined experimentally through entirely reverse strain-controlled tests in which the strain amplitude is constant [ 30 ,  31 – 32 ]. The LCF tests are conducted using a 100-kN capacity Shimadzu Servopulser E model electrohydraulic testing system at room temperature according to ASTM E606M-12 (Standard Test Method for Strain-controlled Fatigue Testing) [ 33 ]. The LCF specimens (Fig.  6 ) with a gauge length of 28 mm and a diameter of 10 mm are processed and polished. The LCF tests under strain control are performed using a sinusoidal waveform with strain ratios (R) of − 1 and a frequency of 5 Hz. Fig. 6 Dimension of the specimen for the fatigue test (mm)

sections.heading: Microstructural Characterisation
paragraphs: The microstructural examination of the forged and welded specimens is conducted by Olympus GX41 model inverted optical microscope. Prior to the microstructural examination, specimens are sectioned, ground with SiC papers (up to 1200 grit) and then mechanically polished with 1 μm alumina solution. Finally, specimens are etched with 3% Nital solution. The ASTM grain size numbers of the specimens are calculated according to the ASTM E112 (Standard Test Methods for Determining Average Grain Size) [ 34 ] at 100X magnification with Olympus Stream Image analysis software.

sections.heading: Wear Tests
paragraphs: For wear tests, disc-type specimens with a diameter of 50 mm and height of 10 mm are cut from the forged and welded samples. Before tests, the surfaces of specimens are ground and polished. The wear tests are performed utilising a UTS Tribolog tribometer with reciprocating ball-on-disc mode according to the ASTM G133 (Standard Test Method for Linearly Reciprocating Ball-on-Flat Sliding Wear) [ 35 ]. For the abrasive wear tests, a WC ball (6 mm diameter) is attached to the load arm and placed perpendicular to the specimen. Tests are conducted at room temperature in dry sliding conditions in a laboratory atmosphere with a relative humidity of 70%. The frequency, stroke length, sliding speed and sliding distance are 5 Hz, 10 mm, 100 mm/s and 10 m, respectively. The friction force and coefficient of friction between the ball and the test specimen are recorded continuously during the tests. The cross-sectional area of the wear craters is examined by a Nanomap LS stylus profilometer [ 36 ].

sections.heading: Microstructural Analysis
paragraphs: The optical micrographs of transverse and longitudinal sections for forged samples are shown in Fig.  7 . The microstructures of forged samples exhibit typical medium carbon steel microstructure: pearlite (dark phases) and ferrite (light phases). Homogenous microstructure with almost no defects is observed for forged samples. The only difference between the microstructures of single and double-forged stem regions seems to be the grain sizes. Double-forged stem regions have finer grains (higher ASTM grain size) compared to single forged stem regions (lower ASTM grain size) [ 37 ]. The microstructures of welded samples (Fig.  8 ) are also examined. HAZ region exhibits a finer microstructure as expected. Welding imperfections such as porosity, shrinkage and cracks are not detected in the microstructures [ 38 ]. Fig. 7 Microstructures and grain size analysis of the forged samples Fig. 8 Microstructures of the welded sample from different zones

The mechanism of friction welding is composed of two main stages: friction and forging stages. The heat is developed in the friction stage, and the specimens are joined and cooled in the forging stage. In the friction stage, as the specimens contact each other, friction takes place between the contacting surfaces, and strong adhesion occurs. As friction continues, the frictional heat input increases and steels start to transfer from one surface to another. Then, steel is plasticized, and a continuous layer is formed. The bonding mechanism in medium carbon non-alloyed steels, which is used in the present study, is not as complex as joining dissimilar metals or high-carbon alloyed steels. At the interface, segregation, diffusion, intermetallic formation and carbide formation can occur. However, in the present study, similar steels having similar compositions are joined together with friction welding. The microscopic analysis of welded specimens reveals that the regions are composed of ferrite and pearlite phases. The difference between the microstructures is the grain size of the regions. Base metal, weld zone and HAZ regions are composed of the same phases (ferrite-pearlite), but the average grain sizes vary in these regions. In addition, the HAZ region exhibits a bimodal distribution of grain size. HAZ region is placed adjacent to the weld zone and is composed of two regions: (i) intercritical region with coarse grains and (ii) subcritical regions with relatively fine grains. The intercritical region encounters the highest temperature. In this region, specimens may be exposed to temperatures in a two-phase (ferrite + austenite) region. Pearlite transforms to austenite during heating, while austenite transforms to pearlite during cooling. On the other hand, in the subcritical region, fine-grained microstructure is formed due to high cooling rates [ 21 ,  22 – 23 ].

sections.heading: Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: The results of the tensile tests for forged and welded specimens are shown in Table  4 . Compared to welded sample, forged samples possess substantially higher tensile and yield strength values. In addition, sample F2, which is double-forged, has higher tensile and yield strength values than sample F1. As given in Table  5 , the mean microhardness value for the forged sample is also higher than that of welded one. Similar to the results of tensile tests, the double-forged region of the forged specimen is relatively harder than single forged region. The finer microstructure in the double-forged region results in lower ductility, higher hardness, higher tensile and yield strength. Table 4 Tensile test results of the forged and welded samples Samples Tensile strength (N/mm 2 ) Yield strength (N/mm 2 ) Elongation at break (%) Reduction of area (%) Impact energy (J) Forged sample F1 827 773 7.8 23.5 9.4 Forged sample F2 899 845 5.8 17.0 13.1 Welded part 662 364 14.3 37.5 7.7 Table 5 Microhardness measurements of the forged and welded sample from locations 1, 2, 3 and 4 Hardness depth (mm) Location 1 of forged sample (HV0,01) Location 2 of forged sample (HV0,01) Location 3 of welded sample (HV0,01) Location 4 of welded sample (HV0,01) 0.25 266 269 190 180 4 272 281 170 160 8 269 278 160 150 12 260 279 150 140 16 261 274 140 120

For welded sample, the Vickers microhardness distribution throughout the welding region is plotted in the form of a colour map (Fig.  9 ). The maximum hardness values are observed in the regions close to the welding region. There are no important differences in the regions nearly 5 mm away from the weld centre. The hardness gradually decreases with increase in distance from the weld region. The maximum hardness values in the weld region can be ascribed to the formation of the microstructure close to the weld region owing to the heat input and extensive plastic deformation. Structural features such as segregation of elements, increased dislocation density, grain refinement and work hardening may cause the highest microhardness values around the weld region [ 38 ]. In addition, the impact energy of the forged specimens is higher than that of the welded specimen. Fig. 9 Microhardness measurements of the welded sample and hardness map of the welded zone

The typical shear stress versus shear strain curves of the warm–cold forged and friction-welded samples are shown in Fig.  10 . Compared to the friction-welded specimen, the forged specimen also has better shear mechanical properties. The shear strength of the forged specimen is 10% higher than that of the welded specimen. Fig. 10 Shear stress versus shear strain curves of the warm–cold forged and friction-welded samples

sections.heading: Fatigue Properties
paragraphs: Maximum tensile stress versus the number of cycles to failure for forged and welded samples are shown in Fig.  11 . At the first cycles of fatigue tests, stress increases and reaches a stable value as the test proceeds. The forged sample has markedly higher stress (nearly 1.5 times) and LCF life values than the welded sample. From the LCF fatigue tests, the fatigue lives for forged and welded samples are estimated to be 1729 and 1386 cycles, respectively. These results show that the fatigue life of forged inner CVJ is significantly increased compared to the welded counterpart. Fig. 11 LCF curves of the warm–cold forged and friction-welded samples

sections.heading: Wear Properties
paragraphs: Figure  12  shows the wear volume profile of all specimens, along with optical micrographs showing the worn surfaces. The variation of volume loss is also calculated from the wear tracks of all specimens, and the results are shown in Fig.  13 . Among investigated specimens, the friction-welded one (Fig.  13 c) exhibits the widest (475 µm) and the deepest (8.5 µm) wear track. On the other hand, the wear track of the double-forged region of the warm–cold forged specimen (Fig.  13 a) possesses the narrowest width (357 µm) and lowest depth (5.0 µm). In addition, the friction-welded specimen shows the highest volume loss (lowest wear resistance) compared to warm–cold forged ones. Interestingly, the double-forged region of the forged specimen exhibits the minimum volume loss (maximum wear resistance). The results of the wear tests imply that mechanical properties such as strength and hardness have an essential effect on wear resistance. Regarding the highest hardness, tensile and yield strength values of the double-forged region of the forged specimen, the highest wear resistance with the lowest volume loss is observed. The volume loss of the friction-welded specimen is 1.4 and 2.3 times higher than those for double-forged region and single forged region of forged specimens, respectively. Fig. 12 2D wear profile scanned along the vertical direction of wear tracks and optical micrographs (100X) showing the worn surfaces of  a  double-forged region,  b  single forged region and  c  friction-welded specimens Fig. 13 The changes in volume loss of warm–cold forged and friction-welded samples

A similar effect of hardness and strength on the wear resistance of several metallic materials has also been reported in previous studies [ 39 ,  40 ,  41 – 42 ]. Higher hardness or strength hinders the material removal from the contacting surfaces during dry sliding. Therefore, the volume loss of the specimens reduces with increase in hardness or strength [ 39 ,  43 ]. The best wear resistance with minimum volume loss is observed for the double-forged region, which exhibits the finest microstructure and highest hardness and strength values.

As a comparison, a considerable amount of plastic strain (deformation) is applied to the specimens during cold forging. The induced plastic strain makes the specimen to be deformed. This phenomenon is called strain (work) hardening. With increase in deformation rate, dislocation density considerably increases, and dislocation motion becomes more difficult. Hindering dislocation motion results in improves strength/hardness and reduced ductility. On the other hand, steels become red hot during friction welding due to the heat input. With increase in rotational speed, the amount of frictional heat greatly increases; thus, softening can occur [ 6 ,  21 ,  22 – 23 ].

sections.heading: Production Cost-Efficiency
paragraphs: In recent years, the automotive industry has shifted towards manufacturing automobile parts that have better performance, reduced weight, reduced cost and are suitable for safety and environmental concerns. In this manner, two important strategies are applied (i) replacement of conventional metals such as steels or cast irons with lightweight materials such as aluminium alloys or composites, and (ii) redesigning of the operating processes. Despite common tendency, safety-relevant automobile components such as CVJs are still manufactured with relatively high-density metals (steels). Therefore, in today’s competitive automotive industry, the production of structural safety components such as CVJs with high performance, reduced weight, and reduced cost is very significant. In this sense, high-quality products with reduced cost can be manufactured by applying the following strategies: (i) decreased material consumption and (ii) elimination of some operation steps if possible [ 44 ,  45 ]. Thus, in the present study, a comparative analysis (see Fig.  14 ) of warm–cold forged and friction-welded inner CVJs with long stems is performed based on the following evaluations: operation steps from beginning to the final part, product weight of the starting billet, labour cost and number of inner CVJs produced per day. Eventually, all these inputs were taken into account to calculate the production cost per piece. Fig. 14 Schematic representation of the process flow charts of friction welding and warm & cold forging operations

Significant improvements in terms of cost-effectiveness are detected in the warm–cold forging process. The production of inner CVJs with friction welding and warm–cold forging takes place with 27 and 22 operations, respectively. For the friction-welded version, before the friction welding process, the CVJ and the stem side are independently processed with 7 and 2 operations, respectively. Then, the CVJ and the stem parts are friction-welded and processed with 17 additional operations. However, for the warm–cold forged inner CVJs, the number of operation steps is reduced since the CVJ and the stem parts are already unified and processed simultaneously for all manufacturing steps.

Compared to friction-welded, significant material saving is observed for warm–cold forged conditions. The weights of inner CVJs produced by friction welding and warm–cold forging are 4600 g and 4240 g, respectively. Moreover, the total number of inner CVJs produced by friction welding is 200–250 parts per day, while the number of warm–cold forged inner CVJs is four times higher (800–1200 parts per day). The labour cost may vary depending on the factory and the country; in this case, the labour cost is kept average for Türkiye standards. It cannot be excluded from the comparison since the labour cost is also different for friction welding and forging operations. Reduced weight, decreased number of operations and increased number of parts significantly decrease production costs and increase efficiency. The total production cost of warm–cold forged products is 13% lower than that of friction-welded ones.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The microstructures, mechanical properties, torsion, fatigue properties, wear behaviour and cost-efficiency of warm–cold forged and friction-welded inner CVJs with long stems are compared, and the following conclusions are obtained. The microstructure of the forged specimens is more uniform than that of welded specimens. The forged specimens exhibit superior mechanical properties: increased hardness, yield and ultimate tensile strength values. The torsion (higher shear strength) and fatigue properties (relatively longer LCF life) of forged ones are also better. The forged specimens exhibit much lower wear volume loss (thinner width and lower depth of wear track), resulting in higher wear resistance. Cost-effective (material saving, reduced number of operations and increased yield) CVJs can easily be produced by warm–cold forging process.
